name: Actual run: eight voice AI interviews
request: Do the eight interviews support the three hypotheses H1 to H3 about voice AI customer support?

picks.name: Definitional analysis
picks.reason: The hypotheses use terms (more satisfying, traditional voice automation, hang up immediately, immediately ask for a human) that need fixed working definitions before any quote can count for or against them.

picks.name: Hypothesis tree
picks.reason: Each hypothesis is a broad claim. Splitting it into sub-claims that must all hold shows which quote bears on which part.

picks.name: Framework analysis
picks.reason: A participant by hypothesis matrix gives a visible base for reading across the eight participants and shows where they disagree.

picks.name: Analysis of competing hypotheses
picks.reason: Rating each quote against rival readings of each hypothesis shows which quotes discriminate and which fit every reading. It reaches the associate level.

picks.name: Comparative case study
picks.reason: Treating each participant as a case with the same questions shows consistent patterns and deviant cases for each hypothesis.

picks.name: Absence analysis
picks.reason: The material quotes only some participants and some scenarios. This separates silence from evidence against.

picks.name: Quality of information check
picks.reason: All quotes come from one source (one study, one prompt set). This shows which findings rest on a single voice and what is missing.

picks.name: Disconfirmation search
picks.reason: A deliberate search for statements that contradict each hypothesis tests the readings that look supported.

picks.name: Source-span and quotation check by code
picks.reason: Every quote the analyses use must be confirmed by string match to exist in the source.

picks.name: Sensitivity analysis
picks.reason: Re-running the verdicts after dropping single participants or changing a definition shows whether a verdict reverses on eight people.

picks.name: Cognitive bias checks and debiasing
picks.reason: A bias check guards against confirmation of the stated hypotheses and over-weighting of vivid quotes.

picks.name: Independent human review of model output
picks.reason: A second person who did not build the analysis should review the verdicts and be able to overrule them.

gaps: No listed technique supplies a statistical test of association, which ten quotes from eight participants could not support. The associate claim therefore reads as patterns within this sample only.

held.name: Independent human review of model output

check.name: Source-span and quotation check by code

results.CM1-05:
# Comparative case study: eight interviews against H1 to H3

Each participant is a case asked the same three questions. H1: is voice AI more satisfying than earlier automation? H2: would they hang up on learning it is an AI? H3: would they ask for a human at once? Cells use only the quotes. P8 and P9 have no quotes.

| Case | H1 | H2 | H3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Mixed: Q1 "pretty dynamic"; Q6 annoyed | No evidence | Unclear (Q6) |
| P2 | Supportive (Q2), no comparison | No evidence | No evidence |
| P3 | Supportive (Q3) | No evidence | No evidence |
| P4 | Supportive after a delay (Q5) | No evidence | Would, at first (Q5, Q9) |
| P5 | Against, accident scenario (Q7) | Conditional hang-up (Q10) | Would ask (Q10) |
| P10 | Against, voice and accent (Q4) | Would hang up at the intro (Q8) | No evidence |
| P8, P9 | No quotes | No quotes | No quotes |

## Consistent patterns

- H1: P1 to P4 react positively, but only P1 compares with earlier systems, and that comparison is with chatbots, not voice automation. The praise describes the AI, not a ranking.
- Negative reactions (P5, P10, P1 in Q6) concern the voice, the accent, the length of the introduction and a stressful scenario.

## Deviant cases

- P10 and P5 say they would hang up (Q8, Q10), against H2.
- P4 and P5 say they would ask for a human (Q5, Q9, Q10), against H3. P4's wish fades as the call continues.

Only these participants speak to H2 or H3, and all point against the hypotheses. Four cases are silent on them. H1 has the most support, but it rests on four cases and a weak comparison.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique assumes each case was chosen for a stated reason. The material says only that some participants are quoted, so selection could favour either side. Most cells are empty because each quote addressed one question at most. Every statement reacts to prerecorded scenarios, and several are hypothetical ("would have"). Nothing here extends beyond this sample.

## Alternative explanations

The negative H2 and H3 cases may reflect the scenario and not the technology: P5 refers to a car accident and P10 to a long introduction. The positive H1 reactions may reflect a good recording, not voice AI in general. Vivid quotes may also have been chosen, overstating both sides.
results.CM1-14:
# Absence analysis: what the quotes leave out

## Reference structure used

The reference structure is the one the material itself states: four prerecorded scenarios (motor claim lodgement, policy sales, premium disputes, policy cancellation), eight participants (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P8, P9, P10) and the three hypotheses H1 to H3. Nothing outside the material was gathered.

## Expected but absent items

| Item | What was expected, and why | Strength of expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Any quote from P8 or P9 | Each of the eight listened to all four scenarios, so each would be expected to have a reaction. However, the material says "Only some participants are quoted", so selection by the compiler explains the gap without any need for a finding about P8 or P9. | Weak |
| Quotes tied to policy sales, premium disputes or policy cancellation | Four scenarios were played, so reactions to each would be expected. Only Q7 names a scenario (a car accident, which matches motor claim lodgement), and it is a hypothetical. Ten quotes are too few to cover four scenarios across eight people. | Weak to moderate |
| A direct comparison with traditional voice automation (H1) | H1 needs a contrast with voice automation. Q1 contrasts the AI with "chat bots", which are text tools. Q2 contrasts it with a "robot voice", and Q3 with having to "repeat yourself", but neither names voice automation. No quote rates satisfaction. | Moderate |
| An observed hang-up or request for a human (H2, H3) | The scenarios were prerecorded, so no participant could hang up or ask for anyone. Q8, Q9 and Q10 are all conditional ("would've", "I would do it"). Observed behaviour was never possible, so its absence says nothing. | Not applicable |
| Disclosure of the AI in the scenarios | H2 and H3 turn on the moment a customer learns it is an AI. Only Q4 ("sounds very much like an AI voice") and Q6 (mention of a human option at the beginning) touch this. The material does not say how or when the scenarios disclosed it. | Moderate |
| Positive quotes from P10, P5 and P4 about the AI | If H1 held broadly, some positive remark from these participants would be expected. P4 gives one (Q5), though it is qualified. P5 and P10 give none in the quoted set, but their quotes may simply be the ones chosen. | Weak |

## Conclusion

Most of these absences are explained by how the material was assembled: a partial set of quotes and prerecorded scenarios. They are limited evidence at best. The strongest expectation is the missing comparison with voice automation, which means the quotes cannot confirm H1 as worded. Q2 and Q3 support only a weaker claim, that P2 and P3 found the AI natural. For H2 and H3, the quotes show intentions, with P10 (Q8) and P5 (Q10) saying they would hang up and P5 (Q10) and P4 (Q9) saying they would ask for a human. These cut against both hypotheses for those three participants.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique assumes the quoted set is a fair sample of what was said. It is not: the compiler chose it and the selection rule is unknown. The technique cannot show what P8 and P9 thought, and cannot show what the full transcripts contain.

## Alternative explanations

The thin coverage of three scenarios may reflect ordinary variation in what participants chose to comment on, not a lack of reaction. The missing voice automation comparison may mean the interview guide never asked for one, so the gap would belong to the design and not to the participants.
results.DM-02:
# Hypothesis tree: do the interviews support H1 to H3?

## Tree

**Main claim: the interviews support H1, H2 and H3.** True only if all three branches are true.

**H1: voice AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation**
- 1a. Participants react positively. Q1 (P1), Q2 (P2) and Q3 (P3) are positive. Q4 (P10), Q6 (P1) and Q7 (P5) are negative. Mixed.
- 1b. Participants rate it above traditional voice automation. Q1 compares with website chatbots, not voice automation. Q2 contrasts it with "a robot voice", a loose proxy. Thin.

**H2: customers do not hang up immediately on learning it is an AI**
- 2a. Participants who learn it is an AI stay on the call. Q8 (P10) says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro." Q10 (P5) says hanging up is likely if no human is offered. Refuted for these two.
- 2b. Other participants stay on the call. No quote says so directly. Not established.

**H3: customers do not immediately ask for a human agent**
- 3a. Participants proceed without asking for a human. Q9 (P4) and Q10 (P5) say they would ask. Q5 (P4) says "I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone" at first. Refuted for these two.
- 3b. Any initial wish for a human fades. Q5 (P4) supports this for one participant only.

## Leaf claims for which no evidence is possible

- 1b in full: no participant heard a traditional voice automation scenario, so no direct comparison exists.
- Actual hang-ups (2a, 2b) and actual requests for a human (3a): the scenarios were prerecorded, so every behaviour quote is a stated intention.
- Any claim about P8 and P9: no quote is given for them.
- Satisfaction on a common measure: no ratings appear in the material.

## Reading

H2 and H3 each have a refuting branch in this sample (P10 for H2; P4 and P5 for H3), so neither holds as stated. H1 has support on 1a only and cannot be tested on 1b.

## Assumptions and limitations

The tree assumes the hypotheses mean what they say, including "immediately", and that stated intentions are a fair guide to behaviour. The material is ten quotes, and how they were selected is unknown. The tree cannot show how common any view is.

## Alternative explanations

The refutations may reflect scenario design, not voice AI itself. Q7 (P5) ties frustration to a car accident, while Q4 (P10) and Q8 (P10) point to an American voice and a long introduction. The praise in Q2 and Q3 may reflect the quality of these particular recordings.
results.FQ-03:
# Definitional analysis of H1 to H3

Each hypothesis depends on terms that can be read more than one way. Findings apply to this sample of eight only.

## Glossary

**Satisfying (H1).** A participant evaluates the AI scenario positively, in their own words, as an experience.
- Borderline: Q2 and Q3 praise human-likeness ("like talking to a real person", "seamless") rather than satisfaction directly. Q5 turns positive only after initial reluctance.

**Traditional voice automation (H1).** Earlier phone systems that respond to menus or keywords.
- Borderline: Q1 compares the AI with chatbots, which this definition excludes. Q2 and Q3 name no system.

**Hang up immediately (H2).** The call ends during the introduction, before any task content.
- Borderline: Q8 ("I would've definitely have hung up at the intro") fits the timing, but it is hypothetical and its stated reason is length, not discovering an AI. Q10's hang-up (Q10) comes only after a human is refused, so it is not immediate.

**Learning it is an AI (H2).** The participant recognises or is told the agent is not human.
- Borderline: Q4 says it "sounds very much like an AI voice", which is recognition by sound. The material does not say whether disclosure occurred.

**Immediately ask for a human (H3).** A request for a human during the introduction, before engaging with the task.
- Borderline: Q9 names the introduction but is hedged ("probably"). Q10's request has no stated timing. Q5 says "I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone", which is a wish, not a request. Q6 mentions the option to ask for a human at the beginning, but P1 does not say they would use it.

## Where answers differ by definition

- H1: Under a strict reading, only Q1 compares with earlier automation, and it is about chatbots. Under a loose reading, Q1 to Q3 support H1 and Q4, Q5 and Q7 complicate it.
- H2: Q8 contradicts H2 only if hypothetical statements count as behaviour.
- H3: Q9 contradicts H3 only if "probably" counts as a request.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique assumed ten quotes suffice to test each definition. It could not count how many of the eight participants fall into each case, because only some are quoted. Every behavioural quote is hypothetical, since participants heard prerecorded scenarios and no one actually hung up or asked.

## Alternative explanations

The positive remarks in Q2 and Q3 may reflect surprise at how human the voice sounded, not satisfaction. The hang-up and human requests in Q8 to Q10 may reflect the length of the introduction or the stressful context of a car accident, not the AI itself.
results.HE1-02:
# Quality of information check: eight voice AI interviews

## Source database

Each participant is one source, rated against H1 to H3. Corroboration means another participant says something consistent.

- **P1** (Q1, Q6). Completeness: medium. Q1 compares the AI with chatbots, not voice automation, so H1 is only partly addressed. Accuracy: self-report. Corroboration: none for Q1 or Q6.
- **P2** (Q2). Completeness: low, one H1 comment. Accuracy: self-report. Corroboration: consistent with Q3 only.
- **P3** (Q3). Completeness: low to medium, one H1 comment. Accuracy: self-report. Corroboration: consistent with Q2.
- **P4** (Q5, Q9). Completeness: medium, covers H3 and a changing reaction. Accuracy: hypothetical ("if it was myself", "If I was gonna do it"). Corroboration: Q9 is consistent with Q10 (P5) on asking for a human.
- **P5** (Q7, Q10). Completeness: medium, covers H1, H2 and H3. Accuracy: hypothetical ("if I was", "would've"). Corroboration: Q10 is consistent with Q9 (P4) and Q8 (P10).
- **P10** (Q4, Q8). Completeness: medium, covers H1 and H2. Accuracy: Q8 is a stated "would've", not observed behaviour. Corroboration: Q8 is partly matched by Q10 (P5, "probably").
- **P8, P9.** No quotes in the material. Completeness, accuracy and corroboration cannot be rated.

## What is known

- Both positive and negative H1 reactions appear (Q2, Q3 against Q4, Q6, Q7). The material does not show whether either group is larger.
- Two quoted participants say they would, or probably would, hang up (Q8, Q10), which counts against H2 for those two.
- Two participants say they would ask for a human (Q9, Q10), which counts against H3 for those two.

## What is unknown

- Any reaction from P8 and P9, and whether the ten quotes represent all eight participants.
- Whether anyone compared the AI with traditional voice automation, which is what H1 names.
- Actual behaviour. Participants only listened to prerecorded scenarios, so H2 and H3 rest on stated intentions.

## Items resting on single-source support

- The chatbot comparison (Q1, P1).
- Annoyance at the human-agent option (Q6, P1).
- The American accent concern (Q4, P10).
- The "cold" voice in a stressful claim (Q7, P5).
- Hanging up at the introduction (Q8, P10) is single-source for that specific point.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique judges only the quotes supplied. It cannot judge full transcripts, quote selection or the unquoted participants, and it gives no verdict on H1 to H3.

## Alternative explanations

The weak support for H2 and H3 may reflect hypothetical phrasing ("would've") rather than real intent. The quotes may also be selected because they are vivid, which would overstate both praise and complaint.
results.HE1-14:
# Framework analysis: eight interviews against H1 to H3

| Case | H1: more satisfying than traditional automation | H2: no immediate hang up on learning it is AI | H3: no immediate request for a human |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Q1: "more, uh, advanced", "pretty dynamic", compared with older chatbots. Q6: annoyed, from past AI agent experience | Empty | Q6: mentions the offer of a human at the beginning; no request described |
| P2 | Q2: "like talking to a real person", "knew exactly what it needed to ask" | Empty | Empty |
| P3 | Q3: "really excellent", "really seamless", no repeating yourself | Empty | Empty |
| P4 | Q5: wanted someone at first, then "a really good process" | Empty | Q5 and Q9: would likely ask at the introduction, though Q5 says the view changed |
| P5 | Q7: "extremely frustrated" in a crash scenario; voice "very cold in clinical" | Q10: would "probably" hang up if no human, then go online (conditional) | Q10: "I would've asked for a human" |
| P8 | Empty | Empty | Empty |
| P9 | Empty | Empty | Empty |
| P10 | Q4: "sounds very much like an AI voice", American, wants a local experience | Q8: "would've definitely have hung up at the intro", reason given is length | Empty |

## Reading across the rows

P2 and P3 are positive on every theme where they have data, and they say nothing on H2 or H3. P4 and P5 are the main sources for H3, and both describe a possible request for a human, so H3 has support against it in this sample. P5 and P10 give the only hang up material (Q10, Q8). P1 is mixed: Q1 is positive and Q6 is negative. P8 and P9 have no quoted data, so they cannot be read either way.

## Reading down the columns

H1: Q1, Q2 and Q3 lean positive, Q4, Q6 and Q7 lean negative, and Q5 moves from negative to positive. Only Q1 and Q2 compare against earlier systems, and Q1 compares with chatbots, not voice automation. H1 is therefore not tested directly.

H2: Q8 and Q10 are both hypothetical and both conditional. Q8 ties the hang up to the length of the introduction, not to learning it was an AI. H2 is weakly contradicted for two participants and silent for six.

H3: Q9 and Q10 run against H3, with Q5 as a partial qualifier. Q6 is ambiguous.

## Empty cells

P8 and P9 are empty throughout. P2 and P3 are empty on H2 and H3, and P1, P4 and P10 are each empty on one theme. The cell pattern shows where quotes exist. It is not a response rate.

## Assumptions and limitations

The matrix assumes the ten quotes are a fair record of each participant, but the material says only some participants are quoted. Empty cells therefore mean "not quoted", not "no view". Coding used the quote text alone, with no transcripts or scenario detail. The matrix cannot show which of the four scenarios each remark concerns, and cannot give frequencies.

## Alternative explanations

The negative H2 and H3 cells may reflect the scenarios, such as the motor claim in Q7, or the specific voice and long introduction (Q4, Q7, Q8), not AI voice support in general. The positive H1 cells may reflect participants judging this one recording against general expectations, not against traditional voice automation. Quote selection may also favour vivid reactions.
results.TC1-13:
# Analysis of competing hypotheses: voice AI interviews

## Hypotheses and rivals

- H1: voice AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation. Rival H1r: it is no more satisfying, or less.
- H2: customers do not hang up immediately on learning it is an AI. Rival H2r: they hang up at or near the start.
- H3: customers do not immediately ask for a human. Rival H3r: they ask for a human at the start.

## Matrix

C = consistent, I = inconsistent, N = not diagnostic. Quotes are classed by their content, and most are hypothetical.

| Quote (participant) | H1 | H1r | H2 | H2r | H3 | H3r |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 (P1) | C | I | N | N | N | N |
| Q2 (P2) | C | I | N | N | N | N |
| Q3 (P3) | C | I | N | N | N | N |
| Q4 (P10) | I | C | N | N | N | N |
| Q5 (P4) | C | I | C | I | I | C |
| Q6 (P1) | N | N | N | N | N | N |
| Q7 (P5) | I | C | N | N | N | N |
| Q8 (P10) | I | C | I | C | N | N |
| Q9 (P4) | N | N | N | N | I | C |
| Q10 (P5) | N | N | N | C | I | C |

## What discriminates

For H1, Q2 and Q3 favour H1 over H1r, while Q4, Q7 and Q8 favour H1r. Q1 compares the AI with website chatbots, not voice automation, so it is only weak support. Q6 does not discriminate, because the annoyance could refer to earlier AI experiences.

For H2, only Q8 (P10: "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro") and Q5 (P4 stays on) separate H2 from H2r. Q10 mentions hanging up only after a human is refused.

For H3, Q5, Q9 and Q10 each count against H3 and for H3r. Q9 says asking for a human at the introduction is "probably where I would do it".

## Fewest inconsistencies

H1 has three inconsistencies and H1r has four, so the evidence is split. H2 and H2r each have one, so the matrix does not separate them. H3r has none, and H3 has three. H3, as worded, is the weakest hypothesis. These three items come from only two participants, P4 and P5.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique assumed that each quote reflects a stable view and that quotes are comparable evidence. Every ranking here rests on single statements. Most are conditional ("would have"), so none records an actual hang-up or request. The material gives no counts and does not say how the ten quotes were chosen. P8 and P9 are not quoted, so the matrix says nothing about them. Q1 compares the AI with chatbots, not voice automation, which limits its bearing on H1. The matrix cannot weight evidence by strength.

## Alternative explanations

The H3 result may reflect scenario type, not attitude to AI. P5 spoke about a car accident, where distress may drive a request for a human. P10's complaint in Q8 is about the length of the introduction and the American voice, so it may not be about AI disclosure at all. The split on H1 may reflect individual differences in prior experience with chatbots, as P1 gives both a positive (Q1) and a negative (Q6) reaction.
results.TC1-16:
# Disconfirmation search on the favoured reading

## Claim under test

The favoured reading across the seven findings is this. In the eight interviews, H1 cannot be tested as worded and has support only for the AI sounding natural. H2 and H3 are contradicted for P10, P5 and P4, but only by hypothetical statements. P8 and P9 contribute nothing.

## Evidence that would refute it (written before searching)

1. A direct comparison with traditional voice automation that favours the AI.
2. A participant who stays on the call after learning it is an AI.
3. Evidence that the hang-up in Q8 or Q10 was immediate and caused by learning it is an AI.
4. A participant who proceeds without asking for a human.
5. Any reaction from P8 or P9.
6. Observed, not hypothetical, behaviour.

## Search and results

The search was one full pass over Q1 to Q10, reading each quote for the item in question. It was a single pass over a small set, so it is shallow.

1. **Partly found.** Q1 compares the AI with website chatbots, and Q2 contrasts it with "a robot voice". Neither names voice automation, so the claim that H1 is untested survives.
2. **Found for one participant.** Q5 (P4): "as the process goes on, you realise it's actually, um, a really good process." This shows a wish for a human fading, so H2 is not contradicted for P4.
3. **Not found, and the reverse was found.** Q8 gives the reason as "it was way too long", and Q10 hangs up only after a human is refused. Neither is an immediate hang-up on learning it is an AI. This weakens "contradicted" for H2.
4. **Not found as a stated behaviour.** Q6 mentions the human option at the beginning but P1 does not say they would use it. Q2 and Q3 are silent on asking.
5. **Not found.** No quote from P8 or P9 exists, so this search could not be run.
6. **Not found.** The scenarios were prerecorded.

## What this means for the claim

The claim survives in a weaker form. H1 is still untested. H2 is the weakest part of the favoured reading: Q8 is hypothetical and gives length as its reason, Q10 is conditional, and Q5 shows one participant staying on. H2 is better described as not supported by the quotes than as contradicted. H3 is more robust. Q9 and Q10 both point to asking for a human, though Q9 is hedged ("probably") and Q10 gives no timing.

Not finding refuting evidence for items 4 to 6 does not confirm the claim. It reflects the limits of the material.

## Assumptions and limitations

The search used only the ten quotes and the seven findings. It cannot see full transcripts or the rule used to select quotes. The refuting items were written after the findings were read, so they may reflect those findings.

## Alternative explanations

Q8 and Q10 may reflect the length of the introduction and the car accident context, not the AI. Q5 may reflect how P4 responded to this recording, not a general pattern.
results.TC1-17:
# Sensitivity analysis: leave-one-out and definition checks

The favoured reading across the seven files is that H1 is not tested directly and is mixed, while H2 and H3 are each contradicted by stated intentions from a few participants (P10 and P5 for H2; P4 and P5 for H3). Each row below changes one assumption only. Only P1, P2, P3, P4, P5 and P10 are quoted, so only they can be dropped.

| Changed assumption | H1 | H2 | H3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original (all quotes, loose definitions) | Mixed: Q1 to Q3 positive, Q4, Q6, Q7 negative; no voice automation comparison | Contradicted by Q8 and Q10 | Contradicted by Q5, Q9, Q10 |
| Drop P1 (Q1, Q6) | Positive Q2, Q3; negative Q4, Q7; still mixed | Unchanged | Unchanged |
| Drop P2 (Q2) | Leans negative (3 against, 2 for) | Unchanged | Unchanged |
| Drop P3 (Q3) | Leans negative (3 against, 2 for) | Unchanged | Unchanged |
| Drop P4 (Q5, Q9) | Unchanged in direction | Unchanged | Only Q10 remains, with no stated timing; weaker but still against |
| Drop P5 (Q7, Q10) | Leans positive (one fewer negative) | Only Q8 remains; still contradicted | Only Q5 (a wish) and Q9 ("probably") remain; hedged |
| Drop P10 (Q4, Q8) | Leans positive | Only Q10 remains; it follows a refused request, so it is not immediate | Unchanged |
| Hang up immediately, strict (during the introduction and because the customer learns it is an AI) | Unchanged | Not contradicted: Q8 gives length, not AI, as its reason; Q10 is not at the start | Unchanged |
| Hang up immediately, loose (any stated hang-up) | Unchanged | Contradicted by Q8 and Q10 | Unchanged |
| Ask for a human immediately, strict (an unhedged request in the introduction) | Unchanged | Unchanged | Not contradicted: Q9 is hedged, Q10 has no timing, Q5 is a wish |
| Ask for a human immediately, loose (any stated wish or request) | Unchanged | Unchanged | Contradicted by Q5, Q9, Q10 |

## Does the conclusion reverse?

Dropping a participant does not reverse any conclusion. H3 weakens when P4 or P5 is removed but still has hedged evidence against it, and H1 stays mixed and untested in every row.

The definitions matter. Under the strict readings, H2 and H3 are no longer contradicted, because no quote meets the strict test. That is a reversal from "contradicted" to "not contradicted", and it does not mean the hypotheses are supported. Dropping P10 alone also removes the only quote that fits the immediate timing for H2.

The favoured reading for H2 and H3 therefore depends on counting hypothetical, hedged or untimed statements as evidence. Rows were varied one at a time, so each change can be traced to its cause.

## Assumptions and limitations

The re-runs use only the ten quotes and the findings' own classifications. P8 and P9 cannot be dropped because they have no quotes. Quote selection is unknown. Leave-one-out tests dependence on individuals, not representativeness. Participants heard prerecorded scenarios, so every behavioural quote is an intention.

## Alternative explanations

The strict-definition result may show that the hypotheses are worded too tightly for hypothetical interview data, not that customers behave differently. Q8 may reflect the length of the introduction, and Q7 the distress of a car accident, so the effects in the original reading may belong to the scenarios and not to voice AI.

synthesis.method: Agreement table, then narrative summary. Pooling of estimates was not offered because no finding estimates a quantity.

legend.D: conflict (points the other way or changes with a definition)

conclusions.text: H1 cannot be tested as worded. No quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation: Q1 compares it with website chatbots and Q2 with a robot voice.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: Nine techniques that read the quotes in different ways agree and their checks passed. They share one material and one model, and the human review sample on the framework analysis was not done.

conclusions.text: Reactions to the AI are mixed. P1 (Q1), P2 (Q2) and P3 (Q3) are positive. P10 (Q4), P1 (Q6) and P5 (Q7) are negative. P4 (Q5) moves from wanting a person to a positive view. The negative remarks concern the voice, the accent, the length of the introduction and a car accident scenario.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Several techniques agree, but the sensitivity analysis shows the overall lean flips when P2 or P3 (toward negative) or P5 or P10 (toward positive) is dropped.

conclusions.text: H2 is neither confirmed nor refuted. P10 (Q8) says they would have hung up at the introduction and P5 (Q10) would probably hang up. Q8 gives the length of the introduction as the reason, and Q10 follows a refused request for a human, so neither is an immediate hang-up on learning it is an AI.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: The first-pass analyses called H2 contradicted. The disconfirmation search and the strict definition run in the sensitivity analysis moved it to not supported, so the verdict depends on whether hypothetical statements count.

conclusions.text: Statements from P4 (Q5, Q9) and P5 (Q10) run against H3: they say they would ask for a human, or wanted one at first. Q9 is hedged ("probably"), Q10 gives no timing and Q5 is a wish that fades.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree, but under a strict definition (an unhedged request during the introduction) no quote contradicts H3, and the evidence comes from two participants.

conclusions.text: P8 and P9 have no quote in the material, so no technique could read a reaction from them. Every statement about hanging up or asking for a human is about prerecorded scenarios, so it is a stated intention.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: This is stated in the material and every technique that touched it reports it the same way.

answer.lead: Not one of the three hypotheses is shown to hold. H1 cannot be tested as worded, and the quotes split between positive and negative reactions. H2 and H3 each have statements from two or three participants that run against them, and whether those count as contradiction depends on how strictly "immediately" is read.
paragraphs: H1 (more satisfying than traditional voice automation): no quote compares the AI with voice automation, so the hypothesis cannot be confirmed or refuted from this material. P1, P2 and P3 describe the AI as dynamic, natural and seamless. P10, P1 (in a second remark) and P5 are negative, and cite the voice, the accent, the introduction and a car accident scenario. Confidence: medium on the split, high that H1 is untested.

H2 (no immediate hang-up on learning it is an AI): P10 and P5 say they would hang up. Neither is an immediate hang-up caused by learning it is an AI. On a loose reading H2 is contradicted by two participants. On a strict reading no quote tests it. Confidence: medium.

H3 (no immediate request for a human): P4 and P5 say they would ask for a human, and P4 says the wish fades as the call goes on. This runs against H3 on a loose reading and does not on a strict one. Confidence: medium.

specs.CM1-14: The result is a list of items that would be expected in the document or comparison set if the claim were true but are absent, with one row per item giving what was expected and why. It states how strong the expectation is for each item and ends with a conclusion that treats the absence as limited evidence unless the expectation is strong.
specs.TC1-17: The result is a table with one row per changed assumption or inclusion rule and the result obtained under each, alongside the original result. It ends by stating whether the conclusion reverses under any row.
specs.FQ-03: The result is a glossary with one entry per ambiguous key term, giving the precise working definition. Each entry lists its borderline cases, and the result names the borderline cases where answers would differ by definition.
specs.CK-17: The result is a pass or fail list with one row per extracted statement, giving the statement, the exact passage it points to, whether that passage exists by string match and whether the passage supports the claim. It ends with the list of statements that failed.
specs.HE1-02: The result is a source database with one row per source, rating its completeness, accuracy and corroboration. It ends with a statement of what is known and what is unknown, and names the items that rest on single-source support.
specs.TC1-16: The result names the claim under test, lists the evidence that would contradict it, and records for each item whether it was found or not found. It states the search used for each item and ends with what the findings mean for the claim.
specs.TC1-13: The result lists the hypotheses and gives a matrix of evidence items against hypotheses with a consistency rating in each cell. It names the evidence items that discriminate between hypotheses and the hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies.
specs.HE1-14: The result is a matrix with one row per case and one column per theme, each cell holding a short summary of the coded data for that case and theme. It notes the empty cells and states what reading across the rows and down the columns shows.
specs.CM1-05: The result is a matrix with one row per case and one column per question asked of every case, each cell holding that case's answer. It names the patterns that are consistent across cases and the deviant cases.
specs.DM-02: The result is a tree in which the main claim is split into the sub-claims that must all be true for it to be true, down to leaf claims. It lists the leaf claims for which no evidence is possible.
